title: Adapa (Standard Babylonian fragments)
author: Anonymous (Babylonian poets)
description: Adapa, Standard Babylonian version: 73 of 97 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (4 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

title: Gospel of Peter (Akhmim codex, pages 2-10)
author: Gospel of Peter
description: The surviving fragment of the Gospel of Peter (trial, crucifixion, burial and resurrection of Jesus), in the Greek of the only manuscript, the Akhmim codex, each chapter linked to the photographed page that carries it.

title: Anzu, Standard Babylonian Tablet I: the theft of the Tablet of Destinies
author: Anonymous (Babylonian poets)
description: The Epic of Anzu, Standard Babylonian Tablet I: 117 of 201 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (4 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

title: Anzu, Standard Babylonian Tablet II: Ninurta goes to war
author: Anonymous (Babylonian poets)
description: The Epic of Anzu, Standard Babylonian Tablet II: 71 of 154 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (4 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

title: Anzu, Standard Babylonian Tablet III: the defeat of Anzu
author: Anonymous (Babylonian poets)
description: The Epic of Anzu, Standard Babylonian Tablet III: 83 of 155 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (3 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

title: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10.6-10.8: happiness and the life of the mind as a divine life
author: Aristotle
description: Aristotle's argument that the highest happiness is the activity of contemplation, a life 'higher than the human level' lived by the divine element in us: 'we ought so far as possible to achieve immortality' (1177b33). Shown on the oldest manuscript, Laur. Plut. 81.11 (10th c.), with its missing text supplied from Paris gr. 1854.

title: Aristotle, Metaphysics 12.6-10 (Lambda): the unmoved mover and the life of god
author: Aristotle
description: Aristotle's account of the first principle: an eternal, unmoved substance whose activity is thought thinking itself; 'the actuality of thought is life, and God is that actuality' (1072b). Shown on Paris gr. 1853, a 10th-century manuscript.

title: Herodotus, Histories 4.184-185: Mount Atlas and the Atlantes
author: Herodotus
description: Herodotus on Mount Atlas, 'the pillar of heaven', and the Atlantes of Libya who eat no living thing and never dream (Histories 4.184-185), on the 10th-century manuscript Laur. Plut. 70.3, fol. 193r-193v.

title: Diodorus of Sicily, Library 3.53-61: the Amazons of Libya and the myths of the Atlantians
author: Diodorus Siculus
description: Diodorus on the Amazons of western Libya who conquered the Atlantians, and the Atlantians' own myths of Uranus, Atlas and the birth of the gods (Library 3.53-61), on Vat. gr. 130.

title: Strabo, Geography 2.3.6: Posidonius on Plato's Atlantis
author: Strabo
description: Strabo reports that Posidonius rightly cited Plato's view that the story of the island of Atlantis, told to Solon by the Egyptian priests, may not be a fiction (Geography 2.3.6), on Paris gr. 1397, fol. 58r.

title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 2.205: lands taken by the sea, 'if we believe Plato' in the Atlantic
author: Pliny the Elder
description: Pliny the Elder on lands swallowed by the sea, first of all, 'if we believe Plato', a vast space where the Atlantic now is (Natural History 2.205), on the 8th-century manuscript Leiden VLF 4, fol. 4v-5r.

title: Aelian, Varia Historia 3.18: Theopompus' tale of Midas and Silenus, the continent beyond Ocean and Meropis
author: Aelian
description: Aelian's summary of Theopompus' story told by Silenus to Midas: a vast continent beyond the Ocean, the cities Eusebes and Machimos, an invasion that turned back at the Hyperboreans, and the Meropes (Varia Historia 3.18), on Paris suppl. gr. 352.

title: Atrahasis, Old Babylonian Tablet I: the rebellion of the gods and the creation of humankind
author: Anonymous (Babylonian poets)
description: Atrahasis, Old Babylonian Tablet I: 31 of 321 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (1 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

title: Atrahasis, Standard Babylonian Tablet I
author: Anonymous (Babylonian poets)
description: Atrahasis, Standard Babylonian Tablet I: 38 of 123 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (3 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

title: Atrahasis, Standard Babylonian Tablet II
author: Anonymous (Babylonian poets)
description: Atrahasis, Standard Babylonian Tablet II: 62 of 116 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (5 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

title: Atrahasis, Standard Babylonian Tablet III
author: Anonymous (Babylonian poets)
description: Atrahasis, Standard Babylonian Tablet III: 54 of 60 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (1 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

title: Berossus, Babyloniaka book 1: Oannes and the creation (Alexander Polyhistor in George Syncellus)
author: Berossus
description: Berossus' account, as summarized by Alexander Polyhistor and copied by George Syncellus, of the records kept at Babylon, the fish-man Oannes who taught writing, cities, laws and agriculture, and the creation of the world by Bel from the body of Omoroka, shown on the two pages of Paris gr. 1711 that carry it.

title: Berossus, Babyloniaka book 2: the ten kings and the flood of Xisouthros (Alexander Polyhistor in George Syncellus)
author: Berossus
description: Berossus on the ten kings who reigned 120 sars (432,000 years) before the flood and on Xisouthros, warned by Kronos in a dream, who buried the writings at Sippar, built a ship, sent out birds and was taken to live with the gods, shown on the two pages of Paris gr. 1711 that carry it.

title: The tower of Babel in Alexander Polyhistor (the Sibyl) and Abydenus (George Syncellus)
author: Berossus
description: Two Greek accounts of the tower of Babylon copied by George Syncellus from the Babylonian tradition: Alexander Polyhistor quoting the Sibyl on a single language, a tower to heaven overthrown by winds, and Titan and Prometheus after the flood; and Abydenus on the first men, proud of their strength, whose tower was thrown down by the winds and who were given many languages, shown on the page of Paris gr. 1711 that carries them.

title: Berossus in Apollodorus: the ten kings before the flood and the fish-men Annedotoi (George Syncellus)
author: Berossus
description: Apollodorus' list, from Berossus, of the ten Chaldean kings from Aloros to Xisouthros with their reigns in sars, and of the fish-men (Oannes, the Annedotoi, Odakon) who came up from the Red Sea, shown on the two pages of Paris gr. 1711 that carry it.

title: Berossus in Abydenus: the kings of the Chaldeans and the flood of Sisithros (George Syncellus)
author: Berossus
description: Abydenus' retelling of Berossus in Ionic Greek: Aloros the shepherd of the people, the sar of 3,600 years, the Annedotoi who came up from the sea, and Sisithros, who hid the writings at Sippar and sailed to Armenia, shown on the page of Paris gr. 1711 that carries it.

title: Berossus in Josephus, Against Apion 1.128-153: Nabopolassar, Nebuchadnezzar and the last kings of Babylon
author: Berossus
description: Josephus quotes Berossus' third book on Nebuchadnezzar's campaign, his building of Babylon and the hanging garden, and the kings after him down to Nabonidus and the capture of Babylon by Cyrus, shown on the four pages of the 10th-century Florence manuscript Laur. Plut. 69.22 that carry it.

title: Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 1: The Despondency of Arjuna
author: Vyasa (attributed)
description: Bhagavad Gita chapter 1 (The Despondency of Arjuna), shown page by page on a Sanskrit manuscript copied in 1794 (Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 559), with the Sanskrit text and Annie Besant's English.

title: Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 2: Yoga by the Sankhya
author: Vyasa (attributed)
description: Bhagavad Gita chapter 2 (Yoga by the Sankhya), shown page by page on a Sanskrit manuscript copied in 1794 (Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 559), with the Sanskrit text and Annie Besant's English.

title: Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 3: The Yoga of Action
author: Vyasa (attributed)
description: Bhagavad Gita chapter 3 (The Yoga of Action), shown page by page on a Sanskrit manuscript copied in 1794 (Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 559), with the Sanskrit text and Annie Besant's English.

author: Shalmaneser III
description: The five tribute captions of Shalmaneser III's Black Obelisk (about 825 BCE), including the tribute of Jehu of Israel, with ORACC's Akkadian and English and photographs of the four sides.

title: 1 Clement (Letter of the Church of Rome to the Corinthians), on Codex Alexandrinus
author: Clement of Rome
description: The letter of the church at Rome to the church at Corinth, traditionally ascribed to Clement of Rome (c. 96 AD), shown chapter by chapter on the pages of Codex Alexandrinus (5th c.), with the lost chapters 57-63 on Codex Hierosolymitanus 54 (1056).

title: 2 Clement (an early Christian sermon), on Codex Alexandrinus
author: 2 Clement (anonymous preacher)
description: The oldest surviving Christian sermon outside the New Testament, transmitted as Clement's second letter to the Corinthians, shown chapter by chapter on Codex Alexandrinus (5th c.) and, after 12.5 where Alexandrinus breaks off, on Codex Hierosolymitanus 54 (1056).

title: Code of Hammurabi: Prologue (obverse, columns i-v)
author: Hammurabi
description: The prologue of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE), in which Hammurabi names the gods who called him to rule and the cities he cared for, shown column by column on the Louvre stele.

title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 1-65 (obverse, columns v-xvi)
author: Hammurabi
description: Laws 1-65 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): false accusation and witnesses, judges, theft and receiving, kidnapping, runaway slaves, burglary and robbery, the fiefs of soldiers and tax-gatherers, fields, gardens, irrigation, and the leasing of orchards. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 100-149 (reverse, columns i-ix)
author: Hammurabi
description: Laws 100-149 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): merchants and their agents, wine-sellers, debt, pledges and deposits, slander, adultery, marriage, the wives of captives, divorce and the sick wife. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 150-199 (reverse, columns ix-xvii)
author: Hammurabi
description: Laws 150-199 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): gifts to wives, debts of husband and wife, incest, betrothal and the marriage settlement, dowries, inheritance, children of slave women, priestesses' shares, adoption, and bodily injury. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 200-249 (reverse, columns xvii-xxi)
author: Hammurabi
description: Laws 200-249 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): bodily injury and its payments, physicians, veterinary surgeons, branders, builders, boatmen, and hired oxen. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 250-282 (reverse, columns xxi-xxiii)
author: Hammurabi
description: Laws 250-282 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): the goring ox, the hire of oxen, farm hands and herdsmen, theft of farm implements, wages of labourers and craftsmen, hire of boats, and the sale of slaves. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

title: Code of Hammurabi: Epilogue (reverse, columns xxiv-xxviii)
author: Hammurabi
description: The epilogue of the Code of Hammurabi: the king's charge to later rulers and the curses on anyone who alters the stele, shown column by column on the Louvre stele.

title: Corpus Hermeticum I: Poimandres
author: Hermes Trismegistus (attributed)
description: The first Hermetic treatise: the vision of Poimandres, the divine Mind, on the making of the world, the fall of the archetypal Man and the soul's ascent through the seven spheres to God, shown complete on the 14th-century Florence manuscript Laur. Plut. 71.33.

title: Counsels of Wisdom (Babylonian moral advice)
author: Anonymous (Babylonian poets)
description: The Counsels of Wisdom, text: 157 of 159 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (13 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

title: Cuthaean Legend of Naram-Sin (Standard Babylonian version)
author: Anonymous (Babylonian poets)
description: The Cuthaean Legend of Naram-Sin, Standard Babylonian version: 175 of 180 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (7 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

title: Cyrus Cylinder, lines 6-36 (BM 90920)
author: Cyrus II (the Great)
description: The Cyrus Cylinder (after 539 BCE), Cyrus the Great's account of his entry into Babylon and the return of the gods and peoples, lines 6-36 with ARIo's text and translation and photographs of the cylinder.

author: Didache (anonymous)
description: The Didache, an early Christian manual of the late first or early second century, shown chapter by chapter on the ten pages of the only complete Greek manuscript (Jerusalem, 1056).

title: Diodorus Siculus 1.10-13: the first men, the eternal gods and the god-kings of Egypt
author: Diodorus Siculus
description: The Egyptian account in Diodorus of how the first men came into being in Egypt from the mud of the Nile, of the sun and moon as the eternal gods Osiris and Isis, of the elements as gods, and of the earthly gods who ruled Egypt as kings, from Helius or Hephaestus to Cronus and Osiris.

title: Diodorus Siculus 1.14-16: Isis and Osiris as givers of grain, wine and law; Hermes the inventor
author: Diodorus Siculus
description: Isis discovers wheat and barley and gives laws, Osiris founds Thebes and teaches the vine, and Hermes invents letters, music, astronomy and the olive, in Diodorus' account of the Egyptian gods who ruled as kings.

title: Diodorus Siculus 1.17-20: the campaign of Osiris through the inhabited world
author: Diodorus Siculus
description: Osiris leaves Isis to rule Egypt and travels with Anubis, Macedon, Pan, the Muses and the Satyrs through Ethiopia, Arabia and India to Thrace, teaching agriculture and the vine, while Heracles stops the flood of the Nile.

title: Diodorus Siculus 1.21-22: the death of Osiris, the vengeance of Isis and the tombs of the gods
author: Diodorus Siculus
description: Typhon murders Osiris and divides his body into twenty-six pieces; Isis and Horus avenge him, Isis gives each order of priests a share of the burial, and the tombs of Isis and Osiris are shown at Memphis and at Philae.

title: Diodorus Siculus 1.23-29: the age of the gods, the Egyptian Heracles, Isis the healer, the stelae of Isis and Osiris, and the colonies from Egypt
author: Diodorus Siculus
description: The Egyptian claims in Diodorus: more than ten thousand years from Osiris to Alexander, the gods' reigns of 1,200 and 300 years explained as lunar years, the giants, the inscriptions on the stelae of Isis and Osiris, and the colonies said to have gone out from Egypt to Babylon, Argos, Colchis, Judea and Athens.

title: Diodorus Siculus 1.44: gods and heroes for almost 18,000 years, then mortal kings
author: Diodorus Siculus
description: Diodorus' summary of the Egyptian priests' chronology: gods and heroes ruled Egypt for a little less than 18,000 years, the last of them Horus son of Isis, and mortal kings for almost 5,000 years, 470 men and 5 women of native birth besides the Ethiopian, Persian and Macedonian rulers.

title: Herodotus, Histories 2.99-101: Min, Nitocris and the 330 kings
author: Herodotus
description: Herodotus begins the Egyptian priests' history of their kings: Min, the first king, who dammed the Nile and founded Memphis; the 330 kings after him read out from a papyrus roll, among them the queen Nitocris; and Moeris, who built the lake.

title: Herodotus, Histories 2.102-110: Sesostris, the conqueror king
author: Herodotus
description: The campaigns of Sesostris by sea and land through Asia and into Europe, the pillars he set up, the Colchians as Egyptian settlers, the plot of his brother at Daphnae, the canals dug by his captives, and his statues at the temple of Hephaestus.

title: Herodotus, Histories 2.111: Pheros, the blind king
author: Herodotus
description: Pheros, son of Sesostris, who threw a spear into the flooding Nile, was struck blind for ten years, and recovered his sight as the oracle of Buto foretold.

title: Herodotus, Histories 2.112-120: Proteus, and Helen in Egypt
author: Herodotus
description: The priests' account of Proteus of Memphis, who detained Helen and the stolen treasure when Paris was driven to Egypt, of Menelaus' visit, and Herodotus' argument that Homer knew this version and that Helen was never at Troy.

title: Herodotus, Histories 2.121-123: Rhampsinitus, the treasure-thief, and the descent to the underworld
author: Herodotus
description: Rhampsinitus and the tale of the builder's sons who robbed his treasury, his journey alive to the underworld where he played dice with Demeter, and the Egyptian teaching on the immortality and migration of the soul.

title: Herodotus, Histories 2.124-128: Cheops and Chephren, the builders of the pyramids
author: Herodotus
description: Cheops, who closed the temples and set all Egyptians to building the Great Pyramid, its construction by stages and its cost in radishes, onions and garlic, and his brother Chephren's pyramid; 106 years of oppression.

title: Herodotus, Histories 2.129-135: Mycerinus, the oracle of six years, and Rhodopis
author: Herodotus
description: Mycerinus, who reopened the temples and judged justly, his daughter buried in a golden cow at Sais, the oracle that gave him six more years, his pyramid, and the story of the courtesan Rhodopis.

title: Herodotus, Histories 2.136: Asychis and the brick pyramid
author: Herodotus
description: Asychis, who built the eastern gateway of the temple of Hephaestus, made a law of loans on the security of a father's mummy, and built a pyramid of brick.

title: Herodotus, Histories 2.137-140: Anysis the blind and Sabacos the Ethiopian
author: Herodotus
description: The blind king Anysis, the fifty-year rule of the Ethiopian Sabacos who raised the cities on mounds, his dream and withdrawal, and Anysis' return from the marshes.

title: Herodotus, Histories 2.141: Sethos and the army of Sennacherib
author: Herodotus
description: Sethos, priest of Hephaestus, whose army of shopkeepers and craftsmen faced Sennacherib at Pelusium, where mice gnawed the enemy's quivers, bowstrings and shield-straps in the night.

title: Herodotus, Histories 2.142-146: The priests' chronology: 341 generations and 11,340 years
author: Herodotus
description: The priests' reckoning from the first king to Sethos: 341 generations of kings and high priests, 11,340 years without a god in human form, in which the sun four times rose out of its usual place; the 345 wooden statues shown to Hecataeus at Thebes; and the ages of Heracles, Dionysus and Pan.

author: Plato

title: Plato, Phaedo 78b-84b: the soul's kinship with the divine
author: Plato

title: Plato, Laws 3.676a-679e: the floods and the survivors on the mountains
author: Plato

title: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Nero, the fire of Rome and the Christians
author: Tacitus
description: Tacitus' account of Nero blaming the Christians for the fire of Rome in 64 AD, with the earliest Roman mention of Christ's execution under Pontius Pilate, shown on the 11th-century manuscript that alone preserves this part of the Annals.

title: Suetonius, Claudius 25.4: the Jews expelled from Rome 'at the instigation of Chrestus'
author: Suetonius
description: Suetonius' one-sentence notice that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were rioting 'at the instigation of Chrestus', shown on an 11th-century manuscript page.

title: Suetonius, Nero 16.2: 'punishment was inflicted on the Christians'
author: Suetonius
description: Suetonius lists the punishment of the Christians, 'a class of men given to a new and mischievous superstition', among Nero's measures, shown on an 11th-century manuscript page.

title: The Rosetta Stone: Greek text of the Memphis decree (complete, lines 1-54)
author: Synod of Egyptian priests at Memphis
description: The complete Greek text of the Rosetta Stone (196 BCE), the priests' decree for Ptolemy V, line by line on the photograph of the stone, with Budge's 1904 English.

title: Sanchuniathon and Philo of Byblos: Porphyry's testimony and Philo's preface (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.9.20-30)
author: Philo of Byblos
description: Eusebius introduces Sanchuniathon of Berytus, older than the Trojan War, whose Phoenician History Philo of Byblos translated into Greek; Porphyry's testimony that he drew on the records of the priest Hierombalus; and Philo's preface on Taautus, inventor of writing, and on the later priests who turned history into allegory.

title: Sanchuniathon: the Phoenician cosmogony and the first worship (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.1-8)
author: Philo of Byblos
description: The beginning of all things in Philo's translation of Sanchuniathon: dark air and chaos, the wind's desire, Mot and the egg-shaped Zophasemin, the 'observers of heaven', thunder waking the first living things, and the first men who worshipped the plants of the earth and the sun as Beelsamen, lord of heaven.

title: Sanchuniathon: the first generations and the inventors of the arts (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.9-14)
author: Philo of Byblos
description: The generations after Aeon and Protogonus: Light, Fire and Flame who discovered fire, the giants who gave their names to Lebanon and Mount Cassius, Hypsuranius who built huts at Tyre and Ousoos who first went to sea, Chrysor who invented iron-working and sailing, the builders of brick, the shepherds, Misor and Sydyk who found salt, and Taautus who invented writing.

title: Sanchuniathon: Uranus, Ge and the reign of Kronos (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.15-30)
author: Philo of Byblos
description: Uranus and Ge, the war of their son Elus or Kronos against his father, the founding of Byblos as the first city, the baetyls or living stones, the children of Kronos and Astarte, Dagon who found grain and the plough, and the mutilation of Uranus near springs and rivers.

title: Sanchuniathon: Astarte, the deeds of Kronos and the symbols of Taautus (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.31-41)
author: Philo of Byblos
description: Astarte with the head of a bull and the star she found and dedicated at Tyre, Kronos' sacrifice of his only son and his gifts of cities, the four eyes and six wings Taautus devised as the insignia of Kronos, the gift of Egypt to Taautus, the records kept by the Cabeiri, and Philo's complaint that the Greeks turned these stories into myth.

title: Philo of Byblos on Taautus, royal sacrifice and the serpent, with Eusebius' conclusion (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.42-55)
author: Philo of Byblos
description: Further passages of Philo: Taautus who first set religion in order, the ancient custom of sacrificing a ruler's beloved son in times of danger, and the serpent, which Taautus held divine, the good daemon of the Phoenicians and the Egyptian Kneph, followed by Eusebius' closing words on the Phoenician theology.

title: Siloam inscription (Hezekiah's tunnel), Istanbul 2195 T
author: Scribe of Hezekiah's tunnel
description: The Siloam inscription from Hezekiah's tunnel in Jerusalem (late 8th century BCE), six lines on the meeting of the two tunnelling teams, with Driver's 1913 Hebrew text and translation and photographs of the stone.

title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)
description: The Sumerian poem of Gilgameš and Enkidu's journey to the cedar mountain to kill the guardian Ḫuwawa, on the Old Babylonian tablets that carry it.

title: Sumerian King List: the Weld-Blundell Prism (WB 444)
author: Sumerian scribes (anonymous)
description: The Sumerian King List on the Weld-Blundell Prism (Ashmolean Museum, c. 1800 BCE), all four faces: the kings before the Flood, the Flood, and the dynasties after it down to Isin.

title: Tel Dan stele (House of David inscription), Israel Museum
author: Hazael of Aram-Damascus (attributed)
description: The Tel Dan stele (9th century BCE), an Aramaean king's victory inscription naming the king of Israel and the 'House of David', line by line with Biran and Naveh's text and translation and a photograph of the stone.

title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
author: Saggil-kinam-ubbib
description: The Babylonian Theodicy, dialogue: 258 of 288 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (10 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
